name: Second Council of Constantinople
informalName: The Fifth Council; the council of the Three Chapters
teaser: Constantinople, 553. Bishops called by the emperor Justinian condemned the Three Chapters, writings tied to Theodore of Mopsuestia, Theodoret and Ibas, while Pope Vigilius, in the city, refused to attend.
knownFor: The council of 553 that condemned the Three Chapters against the ruling of Pope Vigilius, who later gave way, and that Africa, Milan and Istria long refused.
datesNote: 553. The emperor's letter to the council is dated the fourth day before the Nones of May in his twenty-seventh year. The opening on 5 May 553 is Charles Joseph Hefele's dating, which Louis Duchesne also gives. Vigilius's ruling, the Constitutum, is dated the day before the Ides of May, which its editor Otto Günther gives as 14 May 553. No held source gives the date of the closing session
issue: Justinian wanted the Three Chapters condemned: Theodore of Mopsuestia with his writings, Theodoret of Cyrrhus's writings against Cyril of Alexandria, and the letter said to be by Ibas of Edessa to Maris the Persian (the council's sentence; Bossuet, as printed by Henry Percival).
The emperor's case: the followers of Nestorius were bringing their errors into the church through Theodore (the emperor's letter, Session I; the sentence).

Before the council, Evagrius of Epiphania says, the question was put whether it was right to anathematize the dead; Eutychius, then envoy of the bishop of Amasea, answered with King Josiah, who "broke up the sepulchres of those who had long been dead" (Evagrius IV.38).

The other side's case: Facundus of Hermiane says Chalcedon's attackers, the Acephali, were working to have the Chapters condemned, though Chalcedon had judged the letter of Ibas catholic and Theodoret had upheld Leo's Tome there (Facundus, preface). Bossuet says Vigilius and the Western bishops feared the authority of Chalcedon would be destroyed.

On one side stood Justinian, Eutychius and the Eastern bishops; on the other, Vigilius for a time, the African bishops and Facundus. Victor of Tunnuna says the African bishops cut Vigilius off from communion in 550, after he first condemned the Chapters (Victor, under the year his editor gives as 550).
calledBy: The emperor Justinian. The sentence says the bishops met "called thither by the will of God and the bidding of the most religious Emperor", and Victor of Tunnuna says the synod was gathered at the emperor's order. Pope Vigilius did not consent (Hefele)
attended: Hefele names Eutychius of Constantinople as president, with Apollinaris of Alexandria, Domninus of Antioch, three bishops for Eustochius of Jerusalem, and 145 other metropolitans and bishops. No ancient witness held gives a count.
A Vienna manuscript heads its canons "of the 165 holy Fathers"; Percival reports that Hefele and others distrust the figure.
Vigilius was in Constantinople and refused to attend (the emperor's letter; Session VII; Evagrius). Victor of Tunnuna lists him among those present, against the acts.
No list of those present is held. No held source counts the Western or African bishops there.

traditions.name: The Byzantine Imperial Church (Justinianic)
traditions.note: Justinian called the council; Eutychius of Constantinople presided, by Hefele's account, with the bishops of Alexandria and Antioch.

traditions.name: Antiochene Exegetical Christianity
traditions.note: The census row ends about 430, but the council condemned its teachers long after, as the census edge from the Justinianic church already records: Theodore of Mopsuestia and his writings, Theodoret's writings against Cyril, and the letter said to be by Ibas, with all who defend them (the sentence; anathemas XII to XIV).

traditions.name: Latin African Christianity under Byzantium
traditions.note: Victor of Tunnuna tells of African bishops exiled for defending the Three Chapters, himself among them, and of a Roman deacon and an African abbot sent to the Thebaid for opposing the decrees.

traditions.name: The Church of the East under Persia
traditions.note: A synod of the Church of the East, dated to 585 by its editor Jean-Baptiste Chabot, gave a canon to the defence of the books and teaching of "saint Théodore", the Interpreter.

traditions.name: The Roman Church in the Age of Gregory the Great
traditions.note: Vigilius gave way after the council and Pelagius I confirmed it, Percival says. Gregory the Great venerated a fifth council but told Constantius of Milan it touched persons, not the faith.

decided: The Three Chapters are anathematized: "the impious Theodore of Mopsuestia, with his execrable writings, and those things which Theodoret impiously wrote, and the impious letter which is said to be of Ibas, and their defenders" (the sentence, headed Collation VIII in the English extracts).

Fourteen anathemas set out the faith; I to X concern Christ as one person; XI anathematizes Arius, Eunomius, Macedonius, Apollinaris, Nestorius, Eutyches "and Origen"; XII to XIV condemn any who defend Theodore, Theodoret's writings or the letter of Ibas (the capitula; Evagrius counts fourteen chapters).

At the emperor's order the name of Vigilius was to be "no more inserted in the holy diptychs", while the bishops said they would "preserve unity to (ad) the Apostolic See" of Rome (Session VII, given in full only in the Paris manuscript).
Whether the council also passed fifteen anathemas against Origen is disputed: Evagrius says Origen was condemned; Hefele puts the fifteen at a synod of 543; Percival leaves it open.
outcome: Vigilius gave way in a letter to Eutychius dated the sixth day before the Ides of December, condemning Theodore, Theodoret's writings and the letter of Ibas; its genuineness was doubted by Harduin, but "the learned have not generally been of this mind" (the decretal letter and its note, in Percival).

Vigilius died in Sicily on his way home (the Book of the Popes; Victor of Tunnuna, who says he died excommunicated by the whole African church). Pelagius, who as deacon had signed the Constitutum, returned from exile, condemned the Chapters and was made bishop of Rome (Victor).
In Africa, Victor of Tunnuna tells of exiles: Rusticus, a Roman deacon, and Felix, abbot of Gillitanum, to the Thebaid; Frontinus to Antinoe; and Victor himself to Egypt (Victor's chronicle).

Percival says the African opposition died out by 559, Milan was in schism until 571, and part of Istria until the Council of Aquileia in 700. Pope Pelagius II's letter to the Istrian bishops, held in Latin, presses them to give up the Chapters.
In Persia, a synod of the Church of the East, which Chabot dates to 585, gave a canon to the defence of Theodore's books and teaching.

Gregory the Great wrote that he venerated the fifth council, and later told Constantius of Milan that the synod "called by many the fifth" did nothing "with respect to the faith, but only with respect to persons" (Gregory, Letters I.25 and to Constantius).

record.witness: The acts of the Fifth Council: the emperor's letter, Sessions I and VII, the sentence and the fourteen anathemas, in English extracts
record.note: The record of the side that won. The full acts (Mansi, tomus 9) are not held. Percival notes that the Roman and Paris manuscripts differ, and that some of the most injurious things to Vigilius are only in the Paris one.

record.witness: Justinian, letter to the council (read in Session I)
record.note: The emperor who called the council; partisan for it.

record.witness: Vigilius, Constitutum on the Three Chapters (Collectio Avellana, letter 83), and his later letter to Eutychius
record.note: The pope's own ruling against condemning the dead, signed by sixteen bishops, one more by proxy and three Roman clergy; then his letter giving way.

record.witness: Facundus of Hermiane, In Defence of the Three Chapters
record.note: An African bishop at Constantinople during the dispute; the defenders' case in their own words, in Latin.
An African bishop exiled for the Three Chapters, writing year by year; hostile to Vigilius and to the council.

record.witness: Evagrius of Epiphania, Ecclesiastical History IV.38
record.note: Written in the 590s on Chalcedon's side; tells the Eutychius episode and counts fourteen chapters.

record.witness: The Book of the Popes, life of Vigilius (Loomis's English)
record.note: A papal biography Louise Loomis calls full of mistakes; on Vigilius's death in Sicily.
The Church of the East's own synods; its synod dated to 585 defends Theodore. Not an account of the council, but a later synod's answer to it.
Rome's later reception: he venerates a fifth council, and tells Milan it touched persons, not the faith.

record.witness: Charles Joseph Hefele, with Bossuet and Fleury, as printed by Henry R. Percival (Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, series 2, vol. 14)
record.note: Supplies the opening date, the president, the count of 145 bishops and the sequence. Percival's own notes weigh the manuscripts, the Origen question and what followed.
Gives 5 May 553 for the opening and, from a Verona catalogue, 7 June 555 for Vigilius's death.

people.name: Justinian I
people.part: Emperor; called the council and wrote to it; ordered Vigilius's name struck from the diptychs

people.name: Vigilius of Rome
people.part: In the city but refused to attend; issued the Constitutum on 14 May; gave way in a later letter

people.name: Theodoret of Cyrrhus
people.part: Long dead; his writings against Cyril condemned

people.name: Origen
people.part: Long dead; named in the eleventh anathema

people.name: Victor of Tunnuna
people.part: Not present; African bishop exiled for defending the Chapters; chronicler of the resistance

people.name: Theodore of Mopsuestia
people.part: Long dead; he and his writings condemned

people.name: Facundus of Hermiane
people.part: African bishop at Constantinople; wrote twelve books in defence of the Chapters

people.name: Reparatus of Carthage
people.part: Not present; summoned to the capital in 551 and exiled for refusing to condemn the Chapters

people.name: Eutychius of Constantinople
people.part: Bishop of the capital; presided, by Hefele's account; answered the question of cursing the dead

people.name: Ibas of Edessa
people.part: Long dead; the letter said to be his condemned

people.name: Pelagius I of Rome
people.part: As deacon signed the Constitutum; later condemned the Chapters and became bishop of Rome

uncertain: The Library holds only English extracts of the acts. The winners kept the record; the losing side speaks in Vigilius's Constitutum, in Facundus and in Victor of Tunnuna. Percival notes that the manuscripts differ and that the Constantinople copy was tampered with.
The opening date, 5 May 553, is Hefele's and Duchesne's; the emperor's letter itself is dated the fourth day before the Nones of May.
The count of bishops is Hefele's; a Vienna manuscript says 165, which Hefele and others distrust. No ancient witness held gives a count.

Who presided: Hefele names Eutychius. The editor of Gregory's letters in the same series writes of the council as held under the emperor's presidency; Justinian did not sit in it, and his quaestor Constantine spoke for him in Session VII.
Whether Vigilius attended: the acts say he refused; Victor of Tunnuna lists him among those present.

Whether the council passed fifteen anathemas against Origen: Evagrius says Origen was condemned with special anathemas; Hefele assigns the fifteen to a synod of 543; Percival leaves it open, though he holds Origen's name in the eleventh anathema to be genuine.
Whether Vigilius's letter giving way is genuine: Harduin doubted it; Percival says the learned have accepted it. Its date line gives a regnal year that does not match the emperor's letter.

When and where Vigilius died: Sicily, in the Book of the Popes and in Victor; Victor files it under the year his editor gives as 557; Percival gives the end of 554 or the start of 555; Duchesne, from a Verona catalogue, 7 June 555.
